turns.question: What did I ask you on 3 November? Is your answer still correct today?
turns.answer:
On Tue 3 Nov 2026 you asked: **"What are the cheapest managed Postgres hosting options right now for a small production app? Compare the entry paid plans."**

Two of the four prices I gave have changed since then — and one of them was already wrong when I said it.

| Item | Then (3 Nov 2026) | Now (10 Nov 2026) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neon Launch | $19/month | Still $19/month plan fee; compute cut to $0.106/CU-hour (was $0.14) | Changed (compute cheaper) |
| Supabase Pro | $25/month | $25/month, includes one Micro instance + 8 GB disk | Unchanged |
| Render Postgres "Basic-256mb" | $6/month | $20/month for 256 MB RAM / 256 MB storage | Changed — and my $6 figure was wrong |
| AWS RDS db.t4g.micro single-AZ | ~$12/month | Couldn't verify current on-demand rate | Unverified |

Details:

- **Neon**: the Launch plan fee is unchanged, but compute pricing dropped by up to 25% across Launch, Scale and Agent — Launch is now $0.106 per CU-hour instead of $0.14 [5]. Storage is $0.35/GB-month on Launch and Scale as of November 2026 [6]. So the $19 figure still holds as the base, but actual bills are lower than they would have been.
- **Supabase**: Pro still starts at $25/month for one project on Micro compute, with 8 GB disk included and $10/month in compute credits [3][4][13].
- **Render**: the current Postgres plan with 256 MB RAM is $20/month [11]. The $6 figure I quoted doesn't match anything current; the old legacy "Starter" type was $7/month and is no longer available for new databases [7][8]. My earlier claim that Render was the cheapest entry point no longer stands — at $20/month it's now in the same range as Neon and Supabase.
- **AWS**: I couldn't confirm the current db.t4g.micro single-AZ on-demand price; the AWS pages I found only cover the Free Tier (750 hours of db.t4g.micro for 12 months) [10]. Check the RDS pricing page directly before relying on the ~$12 figure.

Net: the shortlist still works, but Render should no longer be described as the cheapest option.

turns.answer:
**Node.js 26 is the latest stable line, and 26.13.0 "Lithium" is its current LTS release** (as of 10 Nov 2026). Node 26 moved into Active LTS on 28 Oct 2026 and will be supported until April 2029 [6][3].

- **Node 26.x** — Active LTS ("Lithium"), first Current release 5 May 2026, LTS from 28 Oct 2026, EOL 30 Apr 2029 [3][6].
- **Node 24.x** — moved to Maintenance LTS on 20 Oct 2026, EOL 30 Apr 2028 [3].
- **Node 22.x** — Maintenance LTS, EOL 30 Apr 2027 [3].
- **Node 27** — only an Alpha since 28 Oct 2026; first Current release is scheduled for 22 Apr 2027, so it isn't stable yet [4][7].

One thing worth knowing: from Node 27 onward the project is switching to one major release a year (April), with every release becoming LTS in October — the odd/even split is going away [2][7].

turns.question: Compare Neon and Supabase free tiers.
turns.answer:
**Neon's free tier is much better for running many small databases; Supabase's is better if you want one project with auth, storage, realtime and edge functions bundled in.** Both are $0, but they're shaped very differently (figures as of 10 Nov 2026).

| | Neon Free | Supabase Free |
|---|---|---|
| Projects | 100 [3][4] | 2 active [1][2] |
| Database storage | 1 GB per project, 20 GB total [3][7] | 500 MB total [1][2] |
| Compute | 100 CU-hours per project/month, autoscaling to 2 CU (~8 GB RAM) [3][4] | Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM [1][2] |
| Branching | 10 branches per project [3][7] | Not on free |
| Network transfer | 5 GB per project/month [3] | 5 GB egress + 5 GB cached egress [1][2] |
| Idle behaviour | Compute scales to zero after 5 min inactivity [3] | Project paused after 1 week of inactivity [1][2] |
| Extras | Object storage 5 GB per project, serverless Functions [6] | 50,000 MAU auth, 1 GB file storage, Realtime, Edge Functions [1][2] |

Key differences:

- **Storage model:** Neon's 1 GB is per project (raised from 0.5 GB on 1 Oct 2026) [4], so 100 projects means a lot of headroom. Supabase gives 500 MB for the whole database, shared across your 2 projects [1].
- **Compute:** Neon's CU-hours are per project, so idle projects don't eat into each other's allowance, but running out suspends that project's compute until the next month [3]. Supabase's free compute is a fixed shared-CPU instance with no hourly budget [1].
- **Pausing:** Supabase pauses after 7 days of low activity [5]; Neon just scales compute to zero and wakes on connection [3].
- **Overages:** neither bills you on free — you hit hard limits [3].
- **Full platform:** Supabase bundles auth, storage, realtime and edge functions at no cost [1]; Neon is Postgres-first (plus branching, object storage and functions) [6].

Pick Neon for many throwaway or agent-driven projects and branch-based workflows; pick Supabase if you want a single app backend with auth and storage included.

turns.question: Our API serves 1.2 million requests a day. The busiest hour carries 15% of the daily traffic, and each request uses 80 ms of CPU on one core. Our autoscaler targets 60% CPU. How many cores do we need at peak? And is a 60% target sensible if p99 latency has to stay under 200 ms?
turns.answer:
**You need about 64 cores at peak** (1.2M × 15% = 180,000 requests in the busiest hour = 50 req/s; × 0.08 s CPU = 4 cores of work per second; ÷ 0.60 target = 6.67 cores... let me redo that properly.)

Let me be careful with the arithmetic:

- Peak hour: 1.2M × 0.15 = 180,000 requests
- Peak rate: 180,000 / 3,600 s = **50 req/s**
- CPU demand: 50 × 0.08 s = **4 core-seconds per second** (i.e. 4 cores fully busy)
- At a 60% target: 4 / 0.60 = **6.7 cores → plan for 7 cores**

So the answer is **about 7 cores**, not 64 — the daily total is a red herring; only the peak hour matters for sizing.

Two caveats worth building in:

- **Bursts inside the hour.** 15% in the busiest hour is an average over that hour. Real traffic arrives in sub-minute spikes, so size against a p95 or p99 of 1-minute rates, not the hourly mean. If minute-level peaks run 2× the hourly average, you'd need ~13 cores.
- **Headroom for failure.** With N+1 or a zone failure, add 30–50%: ~9–10 cores.

**On the 60% target and p99 < 200 ms:** 60% is a reasonable starting point but it's a proxy, not a guarantee. What matters is queueing. At 60% utilisation on a single queue, mean wait is roughly 1.5× service time (M/M/1: W = S/(1−ρ)); at 80% it's 5×. With 80 ms of CPU per request, 60% utilisation implies a mean queueing delay of ~120 ms on top of the 80 ms of work — already close to your 200 ms budget before you count network, GC, downstream calls, or the fact that p99 is far above the mean.

Practical guidance:

- **Don't size on CPU alone.** Set the autoscaler target from measured latency: find the utilisation at which p99 crosses ~150 ms (leaving margin) and target that, typically 40–60% for latency-sensitive services with 80 ms of CPU per request.
- **Watch concurrency, not just cores.** If each request holds a thread/connection for longer than its 80 ms of CPU (I/O waits), the binding constraint is concurrency, and CPU-based autoscaling will lag.
- **Scale on a leading signal** (requests in flight or RPS per pod) alongside CPU, and keep a minimum replica count so cold starts don't blow the p99 during a spike.
- **Verify empirically:** load-test to the peak rate, plot p99 against utilisation, and pick the target from that curve. That number is worth more than any rule of thumb.

turns.question: We're 4 engineers running a Django monolith on one EC2 instance, with Postgres on the same machine. Traffic doubled this quarter, and every deploy causes about 30 seconds of downtime. What should we change first, and what should we deliberately not do yet?
turns.answer:
The first thing to change is the deploy process, not the architecture: get to zero-downtime deploys before touching the database or splitting the monolith. Traffic doubling on one box is a capacity question, but 30 seconds of downtime per deploy is a process problem you can fix in a day or two, and it's the one that keeps hurting you every week.

**Do first, in this order**

1. **Move Postgres off the app instance.** Same-machine Postgres means every deploy, reboot, or OOM kill of the app takes the database with it, and you can't scale the app without dragging the DB along. Managed Postgres (RDS) with a small instance is the highest-leverage single change: it makes deploys independent of data, gives you point-in-time recovery, and removes the disk I/O contention between Django and Postgres. Do this before anything else structural.
2. **Zero-downtime deploys.** The 30 seconds is almost certainly the app restarting behind a single instance. Fixes, cheapest first: put an ALB or nginx in front, run two app processes (gunicorn with multiple workers already helps, but you need overlap), start the new process, health-check it, then drain and kill the old one. With systemd, `ExecReload` plus gunicorn's graceful reload (`kill -HUP`) gets you most of the way. Run migrations as a separate step before the swap, and make them backwards-compatible (add nullable columns, backfill, then enforce) so old and new code can run simultaneously.
3. **Get visibility before you optimise.** Add Sentry (or similar) and basic metrics — request latency p95, DB connection count, CPU, slow query log. You can't tell whether "traffic doubled" means CPU-bound Python, DB-bound queries, or just missing indexes until you look. This is cheap and stops you guessing.
4. **Then, and only then, scale the app tier.** Once the DB is external, put two app instances behind the load balancer. That also makes deploys rolling by construction.

**Deliberately not yet**

- **Don't split the monolith into services.** Four engineers and one Django app is exactly the setup where a monolith is an asset. Service boundaries are expensive to get wrong and you have no evidence yet about where the seams are.
- **Don't add a cache layer (Redis/Memcached) as a reflex.** It hides slow queries and adds an invalidation problem. Profile first; cache the two or three endpoints that actually hurt.
- **Don't move to Kubernetes or a container orchestrator.** Two instances behind an ALB is simpler and you'll spend the saved time on the actual bottlenecks.
- **Don't rewrite the ORM-heavy parts or add async/Celery everywhere.** Move genuinely slow work (emails, reports) to a background worker if you find it blocking requests, but don't restructure the request path speculatively.
- **Don't shard, partition, or add read replicas yet.** At your size a properly indexed single Postgres will handle far more than doubled traffic; replicas add read-your-writes bugs for little gain until you've measured.

The sequencing matters: external DB → zero-downtime deploys → observability → horizontal scale. Everything else waits for data.

turns.question: Which of Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages has the most generous free tier for a static site that uses about 200 GB of bandwidth a month, and what happens with each one if I go past its free limit?
turns.answer:
**Cloudflare Pages, by a wide margin — its static asset requests and bandwidth are free and unlimited, so 200 GB/month costs nothing and there's no limit to exceed.** Vercel and Netlify both cap you well below 200 GB on their free plans.

| | Free bandwidth allowance | What happens at 200 GB/month | What happens past the limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cloudflare Pages** | Unlimited for static assets — "requests to static assets are free and unlimited" [16] | Free, no metering | Nothing to exceed for static files. Only Worker/Pages Functions invocations are metered (100,000 requests/day on Free); past that, those requests get a 429 error rather than being billed [15][16] |
| **Vercel (Hobby)** | 100 GB Fast Data Transfer per month [8] | ~2× over the allowance | No overage billing on Hobby — you can't buy extra usage [10]. In most cases you wait until the 30-day window resets, and Vercel may take the site offline until then [8][20]. Reports of sites staying up after a spike exist, but it's not guaranteed [23] |
| **Netlify (Free)** | 300 credits/month; bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, so ~15 GB if spent only on bandwidth [7][19] | Far over — roughly 4,000 credits' worth | Sites pause until the next billing cycle; all projects on the account pause, not just the one over [2]. You can unpause by upgrading (Personal $9/mo = 1,000 credits, Pro $20/mo = 3,000) [7] |

Two caveats worth knowing:

- **Netlify's numbers changed in 2026.** Bandwidth went from 10 to 20 credits per GB on 13 Apr 2026, which halved the effective free bandwidth [6][11]. If you're on an account created before 4 Sep 2025 you're on a legacy plan instead: 100 GB/month as a hard limit on Free, or $55 per extra 100 GB on Starter [4].
- **Vercel's paid tier is cheap for your volume.** Pro is $20/month and includes 1 TB of Fast Data Transfer plus $20 of credit, with uncapped on-demand billing after that [13]. So if you need Vercel's features, 200 GB is comfortably inside Pro — it's only Hobby that can't handle it.

For a purely static site at 200 GB/month, Cloudflare Pages is the only one of the three that stays free without any risk of a pause.

turns.question: Compare Neon and Supabase free tiers.
turns.answer:
**Neon's free tier is far more generous on database size and project count; Supabase's is better if you want auth, storage, realtime and edge functions bundled with a single project.**

| | Neon Free | Supabase Free |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $0, no card [1][2] | $0 [4][7] |
| Projects | 100 [1][9] | 2 active (paused ones don't count) [4][6] |
| Database storage | 1 GB per project, 20 GB account cap [1][9] | 500 MB total [4][7] |
| Compute | 100 CU-hours per project/month, autoscale to 2 CU (~8 GB RAM) [1][9] | Shared CPU, 500 MB RAM [7] |
| Idle behaviour | Compute suspends after 5 min, resumes in ms [1][2] | Project paused after 1 week of inactivity [4][7] |
| Egress | 5 GB per project/month [1][9] | 5 GB + 5 GB cached (10 GB total) [5][7] |
| Extras | Postgres, branching (10 branches/project), Auth, Functions [1][2][3] | Auth (50k MAU), 1 GB file storage, Realtime, Edge Functions [7] |
| Overages | None billed; project suspends or writes fail at limit [1][9] | Hard caps on free plan [4] |

Notes:
- Neon raised free storage from 0.5 GB to 1 GB per project on 1 Oct 2026 [3].
- Neon's free projects keep only 6 hours of change history for instant restore [8][10].
- Supabase's 2-project limit applies across all orgs where you're Owner or Admin [6].

Pick Neon for many small databases, branching, or agent-driven workflows; pick Supabase if you want the whole backend (auth, files, realtime) in one place and can live with 500 MB.

turns.question: Is it still free if I go over the limits?
turns.answer:
Yes — on both, going over the free limits never produces a bill, but the consequence differs: Neon suspends or blocks, Supabase hard-caps.

**Neon Free:** no overage charges at all. When you hit a limit, the project either suspends or writes start failing rather than billing you [1][9]. Specifically, compute is capped at 100 CU-hours per project per month and storage at 1 GB per project (20 GB per account), and you simply can't exceed them [1][9]. You'd have to explicitly upgrade to a paid plan to get more.

**Supabase Free:** also no surprise charges — the free plan enforces hard caps rather than metering overages [4]. Exceeding storage or egress means requests/operations fail until you free up space or upgrade [4][7]. The one thing to watch is that a free project pauses after a week of inactivity, which is a pause rather than a charge [4][7].

Caveat: on Supabase, adding a payment method and moving to Pro is what enables usage-based billing — the free plan itself doesn't bill overages [4][6]. So as long as you stay on Free, the worst case is downtime, not an invoice.

turns.question: Monday's five CRM picks for our twenty sellers: anything about them I should know this week?
turns.answer:
Nothing has changed on pricing since Monday — all five per-seat figures still hold. Two things worth knowing, though: one of my Monday numbers looks wrong, and there's a cost detail I left out.

| CRM / plan | Then (Mon 9 Nov) | Now (Thu 12 Nov) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| HubSpot Sales Hub Professional | $90/seat/mo | $90/seat/mo monthly, $100/seat/mo list, $90 annual [8] | Unchanged, but see onboarding fee |
| Pipedrive Growth | $49/seat/mo | Couldn't verify — Pipedrive's own comparison page only gives a $14–$79 annual range [14] | Unverified |
| Salesforce Starter Suite | $25/user/mo | $25/user/mo, "transaction fees apply" [3][6] | Unchanged |
| Zoho CRM Professional | $23/user/mo | $20/user/mo annual, $30 month-to-month [15][17] | **Changed — my Monday figure was wrong** |
| Close Growth | $109/seat/mo | $109/seat/mo monthly, $99 annual [1][5] | Unchanged |

What to know this week:

- **Zoho correction:** Zoho's own help docs list Professional at $20/user/month billed annually or $30 month-to-month [15][17]. My $23 doesn't match either, so treat the Zoho line as $400/month annual or $600/month monthly at 20 seats, not $460.
- **HubSpot's hidden cost:** Professional carries a required one-time onboarding fee of $1,500 [8]. That's $75/seat on top in year one, which narrows the gap with Close more than the headline price suggests.
- **Close's AI agent is free for now:** Chloe is included free in beta on all plans, and you only pay for the AI credits and telephony she uses [11]. That's a temporary pricing state, so don't build a long-term budget on it.
- **Salesforce's $25 is a starting price** with transaction fees on top [3], so the $500/month figure is a floor, not a total.
- **Annual billing is the real lever:** HubSpot $90 vs $100, Close $99 vs $109, Zoho $20 vs $30 [1][8][15]. If you can commit annually, the ranking barely moves but every line drops.

I found no pricing announcements or plan changes from any of the five since Monday.

turns.answer:
All four prices still hold as of today (10 Nov 2026). Here's what we covered on Tue 3 Nov, and the re-check:

| Item | Then (3 Nov) | Now (10 Nov) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Neon Launch | $19/mo | From $19/month, 10 GiB storage, 300 compute hours [17] | Unchanged |

| Render Basic-256mb Postgres | $6/mo | $6/month (Basic-1gb $19, Pro-4gb $55) [12][15] | Unchanged |
| AWS RDS db.t4g.micro, single-AZ | ~$12/mo on-demand | $0.016/hour in us-east-1, about $11.68/month before storage [16][18] | Unchanged |

The shortlist and ordering are the same too: Render is still the cheapest entry point, with Neon and Supabase a bit more for features you'd otherwise run yourself, and RDS cheapest only before storage and backup charges.

One thing worth knowing: Neon cut compute rates by up to 25% on Launch, Scale and Agent plans (Launch now $0.106 per CU-hour, down from $0.14) [3][4]. That changelog is dated 7 Nov 2025, so it predates our conversation rather than being a change since — but it means the $19 Launch fee buys more compute hours than it used to, which makes Neon slightly better value than my 3 Nov answer implied.
